messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 69-year-old plumber who has been married to his wife, Linh, for over forty years. He still remembers the week he was taken captive twenty-three years ago, when a routine plumbing job at a warehouse turned into a nightmare. Three men grabbed him as he worked alone in the basement, bound his hands behind his back, and kept him tied to a pipe for four days. The rope cut into his neck, sending a sharp, burning pain that would not stop. He felt nauseous from the fear and the stale air, vomiting into a bucket while the men argued above him. To this day, the memory plays in his mind like a film he cannot pause—the dim light, the sound of their boots, the pressure on his throat. When he tries to explain what happened, the thread of the story slips away; he knows what he endured, but the words simply will not come.

In the months after his release, Minh found himself constantly on edge. The memory itself kept him alert; even at home, he felt a knot in his stomach and a readiness to defend himself, as though the men might burst through the door. He began to detach from the memories, forcing himself to think of something else every time the image surfaced, but the more he pushed it away, the more it returned—a loop of film that played just when he tried to sleep. He also avoided the anniversary of his capture, making sure he was too busy with work to notice the date, yet the memory always found him anyway, often on the day itself or the day before.  

Now, years later, the triggers are everywhere. Being alone with any man—a customer in a basement, a neighbor in the elevator—makes his throat tighten. He recognizes the sick feeling in his stomach and the familiar ache in his neck as soon as a male client asks him to work in a closed room. Those physical sensations immediately pull the memory back into sharp focus, the film rolling once more. In response, he has learned to plan an escape route before entering any new place, checking windows and back doors, telling himself it is just caution. That planning, however, keeps his mind fixed on the possibility of danger; when a man makes a sudden movement near him, Minh’s heart pounds and his body reacts as if the captivity is happening again.  

The memory itself has become a trigger. A quiet evening at home, a fleeting thought about the event, and suddenly his stomach turns and his neck aches. He cannot find words to describe the experience to his wife, so he stays silent, which only makes the memory feel more isolated and more present. His avoidance of anniversaries has also backfired: the more he tries to ignore the date, the more sensitive he becomes to any reminder in the days around it, and every male voice or sudden noise puts him on high alert. That hypervigilance—always scanning for exits, always ready to bolt—has only deepened his sense that danger lurks around every corner, even in his own living room.  

It was Linh who finally urged him to seek help after she found him pacing the kitchen one evening, unable to explain why he could not sit still. What frightens Minh most is not the memory itself but the feeling that he has lost control—that the film will keep playing, the nausea will keep rising, and he will never find the words to make anyone understand. He hopes only to quiet the loop, to feel safe in his own home without having to scan the door.
